title: Theo and the Radiators
premise: Mara Okafor, a piano tuner who reads houses through their radiators, is hired to prepare the decaying Fenwick house for sale and discovers a cache of undelivered letters behind a wardrobe — letters written by Eleanor Fenwick to a lover her family erased, and answered by Mara's own grandmother, whom Eleanor's brother destroyed. As Mara traces the correspondence through the house's pipes and photographs, she must decide whether exposing the truth will save or shatter the last surviving Fenwick, the dying Elias, who has spent sixty years guarding the lie. In the end, Mara delivers the final letter to Elias on his deathbed, forgives the stranger in the photographs — her own grandfather — and lets the house, and its history, go warm.
about_author: Y. M. Dunmore is the pen name of a former building restorer who spent a decade listening to old houses before writing about them. Dunmore lives in a converted mill with a temperamental boiler and writes at the hour when radiators begin to tick.

chapters.title: The Tuner's Ear
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. She arrives at the Fenwick house to tune its ancient piano, reading the radiators' knocks and hisses like a family album. She deploys her perfected smile to end the estate agent's chatter. Beat: guarded competence masking loneliness; the house already feels like it knows her.

chapters.title: Behind the Wardrobe
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. Moving furniture to reach a cold radiator, she finds a cavity stuffed with undelivered letters, tied in ribbon, spanning 1958–1963. The handwriting shifts between two correspondents. Beat: curiosity igniting into compulsion; the first letter names her grandmother's street.

chapters.title: Eleanor's Hand
chapters.summary: Mara's POV, interleaved with letter excerpts. She reads Eleanor Fenwick's fierce, funny voice describing a forbidden love and a brother who 'collects people like debts.' Beat: intimacy with a dead stranger; Mara recognizes the family silence she grew up inside.

chapters.title: The Man in the Photograph
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. A loose photograph falls from the letters: young Eleanor beside a man whose face mirrors her own father's. She cross-checks dates against her grandmother's old address book. Beat: vertigo — the lover may be her grandfather, the erasure may be hers to inherit.

chapters.title: Cold Rooms
chapters.summary: Elias Fenwick's POV, brief and failing. Ninety-one years old, he walks the house at night, touching radiators that no longer work, rehearsing a confession he has abandoned for six decades. Beat: dread and tenderness; he senses someone moving through his secrets.

chapters.title: What the Pipes Remember
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. She maps the house room by room, correlating radiator sounds with events in the letters — a party, a pregnancy, a slammed door. The house becomes testimony. Beat: obsession deepening; her own flat feels increasingly like a place she merely stores herself.

chapters.title: The Smile Fails
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. The estate agent pushes her to finish quickly; her smile doesn't end the conversation this time, and she lies badly about why she needs another week. Beat: her armor cracking; duty to the job versus duty to the dead begins to split.

chapters.title: Letters Never Sent
chapters.summary: Alternating POV: Eleanor's letters grow desperate as her brother intercepts her mail; a reply from Mara's grandmother, Ruth, reveals the two women met once and conspired to keep the child's existence secret. Beat: the love story widens into a conspiracy of women against a powerful man.

chapters.title: Elias Answers the Door
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. She visits Elias under a pretext; he serves tea in a house of cold rooms and watches her too carefully. He mentions the wardrobe unprompted. Beat: cat-and-mouse tenderness; each recognizes the other is holding something.

chapters.title: Power's Arithmetic
chapters.summary: Elias's POV, 1961 flashback. Young Elias destroys his sister's engagement, buys off her lover, and buries the letters — believing himself merciful. Beat: the banality of corruption; power rationalizing itself as protection.

chapters.title: Ruth's Silence
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. She confronts her mother with the letters; her mother reveals Ruth returned from the Fenwick house in 1963 changed, never spoke of it, and made the family promise silence. Beat: generational wound opened; Mara realizes forgiveness was never offered because truth never was.

chapters.title: The Second Cache
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. Following a radiator's dead knock to a sealed flue, she finds Eleanor's diary and proof the child — Mara's father — was born alive and given away. Beat: revelation as grief; the stranger in the photograph becomes flesh, blood, inheritance.

chapters.title: A House Divided Against Its Heat
chapters.summary: Dual POV. Elias learns someone has been in the walls; Mara decides to tell him everything before the sale closes. Their orbits tighten. Beat: rising tension; both know a confrontation is coming and neither can stop preparing for it.

chapters.title: The Confrontation in the Music Room
chapters.summary: Mara and Elias, shared scene. She lays the letters on the piano; he confesses — not to cruelty but to cowardice — and asks what she wants. Beat: climax of truth-telling; anger and pity colliding in a room where the piano finally holds its tune.

chapters.title: Forgiving the Stranger
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. She spends a night with the photographs and letters, composing the forgiveness she cannot feel yet, addressing her grandfather across time. Beat: interior climax; identity reassembling around chosen memory rather than inherited silence.

chapters.title: Time Already Running Out
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. His health collapses; the sale accelerates; lawyers circle. He asks Mara, not his solicitor, to be his executor of one final task. Beat: urgency sharpening every remaining choice; duty and love reversing places.

chapters.title: The Last Letter
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. She writes nothing; instead she delivers Eleanor's final unsent letter — found decades late in the flue — to Elias's hospital bedside and reads it aloud. Beat: emotional peak; the dead woman's voice doing what no living apology could.

chapters.title: What We Owe the Dead
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. Elias dies holding the letter; the family contests nothing because there is no one left to contest it. Mara chooses to publish the correspondence rather than bury it again. Beat: cost acknowledged; truth chosen over comfort, knowing it will hurt living people.

chapters.title: Publication and Backlash
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. The letters appear in a small press edition; a cousin accuses her of grave-robbing; her mother stops calling. Beat: consequence; love against duty resolved painfully, honestly, without vindication.

chapters.title: Reconciliation, Imperfect
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. Her mother arrives unannounced at the empty Fenwick house; they read one letter together in the cold music room and do not resolve everything, but they stay. Beat: quiet repair; forgiveness as practice, not event.

chapters.title: Bleeding the Radiators
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. On the house's final day, she bleeds every radiator herself, releasing trapped air until the pipes run warm and silent, then locks the door for the new owners. Beat: ritual and release; the house's history honored by letting it rest.

chapters.title: Theo
chapters.summary: Final chapter, Mara's POV. She names the child from the letters — Theo, the grandfather she never met — on a new headstone beside Eleanor's, then plays the tuned piano for an empty room. Beat: resolution; identity fully claimed, the smile retired, warmth carried forward instead of kept.
